title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a pedagogically fine-tuned generative AI tutor, LearnLM, can safely and effectively support student learning in real UK secondary school classrooms. The study addresses the broader problem that one-to-one tutoring is highly effective but difficult to scale because of cost and staffing constraints. The authors specifically ask whether AI-supported tutoring can provide reliable pedagogical guidance, improve mathematics learning outcomes, and do so safely under human supervision.

The intervention was implemented on the Eedi mathematics platform. In an exploratory randomized controlled trial, 165 secondary students were assigned either to receive static pre-written hints or interactive tutoring. Within the tutoring arm, individual sessions were further randomized to either a human tutor alone or LearnLM drafting tutoring messages that were reviewed by an expert human tutor before being sent. The paper also includes surveys and semi-structured interviews with tutors and a post-trial student survey, allowing the authors to combine quantitative efficacy evidence with qualitative experience data.

The population consisted of Year 9 and Year 10 students (ages 13-15) from five UK secondary schools using Eedi as part of regular mathematics instruction, along with 17 expert tutors who supervised or delivered tutoring. The trial lasted seven weeks during normal classroom use of a curriculum-aligned online mathematics platform. The study focused on mathematics multiple-choice study units and measured immediate mistake correction, misconception resolution, and transfer to the next study unit. The paper does not concern ChatGPT-generated feedback on student-authored drafts, writing outcomes, writing self-efficacy, plagiarism, overreliance, or other writing-specific secondary outcomes; evidence on those requested topics is absent.

The main conclusion is that supervised LearnLM tutoring was safe, with no harmful content identified in audited messages and very few factual errors, and that it performed at least as well as human tutors on immediate learning outcomes. Students receiving LearnLM-supported tutoring also showed stronger transfer to subsequent mathematics topics than students tutored by humans alone. Tutors reported that LearnLM often generated strong Socratic questions and sometimes supported their own professional learning, although human supervisors were still important for pacing and social-emotional nuance. The authors caution that the study was short, limited to mathematics, and did not measure longer-term cumulative learning effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory randomized controlled trial in authentic secondary classrooms, which is stronger than correlational evidence. However, it is a preprint/tech report with some credibility concerns: modest sample size, session-level crossover between human and AI conditions, limited external outcome measures, and no long-term follow-up.
impact_tier_rationale: The clearest effect is a modest positive transfer advantage for LearnLM tutoring over human tutoring (+5.5 percentage points) and larger advantages for interactive tutoring over static hints on near-term math outcomes. Effects are promising but mostly reported as percentage-point differences rather than standardized impacts, and the transfer interval includes zero.

interventions.use_case: Pedagogically fine-tuned generative AI (LearnLM) drafts Socratic chat messages for secondary school mathematics tutoring on the Eedi platform, with each message reviewed and optionally edited by a human tutor before being sent to students.
Pre-written static hints on the Eedi mathematics platform serve as a non-interactive software-based comparison condition after students answer diagnostic multiple-choice questions incorrectly.

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory classroom RCT with N=165 Year 9-10 students across five UK secondary schools, supervised LearnLM tutoring performed at least as well as human tutoring on immediate math outcomes and showed an advantage on transfer to the next study unit. Students in LearnLM-supported sessions answered second attempts correctly 93.0% (95% credible interval [90.4%, 95.3%]) and resolved misconceptions 95.4% [93.1%, 97.1%]; for transfer, they solved the first question in the next unit at 66.2% [61.1%, 71.2%] versus 60.7% [55.8%, 65.4%] for human tutors, a +5.5 percentage-point difference with interval [-1.4%, +12.4%] and 93.6% posterior probability of superiority.
finding.measure: Math learning outcomes on Eedi diagnostic questions: second-attempt correctness, any correct answer within the same study unit after intervention, and correctness on the first question of the subsequent study unit (knowledge transfer).
finding.effect_size: +5.5 percentage points for knowledge transfer (LearnLM vs human tutor); other outcomes reported as adjusted success-rate differences rather than standardized effect sizes
finding.confidence_interval: Second attempt: [90.4%, 95.3%]; misconception resolution: [93.1%, 97.1%]; transfer difference vs human tutor: [-1.4%, +12.4%]

finding.finding_summary: Static pre-written hints were less effective than interactive tutoring on all measured mathematics outcomes. Students receiving static hints answered second attempts correctly 65.4% [63.8%, 66.9%], resolved misconceptions 86.8% [85.7%, 88.0%], and answered the first question of the next unit correctly 56.2% [54.2%, 58.2%].
finding.measure: Math learning outcomes on Eedi diagnostic questions: second-attempt correctness, misconception resolution within the unit, and correctness on the first question of the next unit.
finding.study_size: N=165 students overall; arm-specific n not reported in outcome section
finding.effect_size: Comparator condition only; no standardized effect size reported

finding.finding_summary: Tutor reports suggested that LearnLM increased tutoring efficiency and capacity, especially by helping tutors support multiple students simultaneously. However, these findings are based on tutor surveys/interviews rather than a rigorous throughput analysis, and the authors explicitly state the RCT design precluded causal measurement of efficiency; post-trial tutor comfort with AI rose from 3.4 to 3.9 out of 5, with 90.0% posterior probability of increase.
finding.measure: Tutor surveys/interviews about perceived efficiency, ability to support multiple students, and self-reported comfort with AI.
finding.effect_size: Mean comfort with AI increased from 3.4 to 3.9 on a 5-point scale; no standardized effect size reported

finding.finding_summary: Student and tutor process data indicate generally positive experience with tutoring, but also note frustration risks from LearnLM's pacing. Students who received interactive tutoring rated support helpfulness at 3.9 out of 5 versus 3.6 for static hints, with 74.9% posterior probability of an advantage for tutoring; interviews also showed tutors frequently edited LearnLM messages to prevent student exasperation, with 44.3% of edits focused on pacing and 19.5% on social-emotional tone.
finding.measure: Post-trial student helpfulness ratings and tutor qualitative coding of message edits related to pacing, tone, and student frustration.
finding.study_size: n=27 student survey responses; n=17 tutors; full corpus of 3,617 drafted messages
finding.effect_size: Helpfulness rating difference of 0.3 points on a 5-point scale; no standardized effect size reported
finding.confidence_interval: Student helpfulness tutoring [3.1, 4.7] vs static hints [2.9, 4.2]
